title: Montaigne
summary: Montaigne was a French Renaissance philosopher who invented the essay. His Essays are an honest, lively observation of himself: he examines his thoughts, habits and shifts of mood in order to understand what it means to be human. His motto is a question: “What do I know?”
onEmotions: Montaigne looked at feelings as an attentive and kindly observer. He was a sceptic: he held that our judgements change along with the body, our mood and circumstances, and that the human being is a changeable, contradictory creature. Instead of being ashamed of this, Montaigne accepted his own changeability as part of human nature. His method was self-observation: looking at his fears, desires and joys with curiosity, without judgement. He believed that each person bears the entire form of the human condition, and that the highest art is knowing how to live and to enjoy one’s own being.

anxiety.text: Montaigne had an odd habit for a philosopher: catching his mind by the hand and asking where it had run off to. Anxiety is one of those escapes: you are already living in a tomorrow that doesn’t exist yet, and it looks dangerous. He described this escape precisely: we are almost never “at home” in ourselves; our fears and desires keep carrying us forward, beyond the present. He also liked to repeat the thought of the Stoic Epictetus: people are troubled not by things themselves but by their opinions about things. His method was to examine himself closely, like a curious object: what exactly am I imagining right now? How much does it resemble what is actually happening? This kind of self-observation doesn’t cancel anxiety, but it brings you back from an imagined future into the room where you are actually sitting.
anxiety.practice: Catch the anxious thought and ask it out loud, as Montaigne asked his mind: “Where have you run off to?” Then name three things in the room where you are actually sitting.

fear.text: “The thing I fear most is fear,” Montaigne admits in an essay titled simply “Of Fear.” If you are frightened right now, you are in good company. In his observation, fear can bind us more tightly than any real misfortune. He collected stories of how fear sometimes gives people wings and sometimes paralyses them, and concluded that the imagination knows how to inflate danger to monstrous size. But Montaigne did not shame the frightened. His approach was to see fear as part of our shared human nature rather than a personal failure. When you name your fear out loud and see that everyone is subject to it, from soldiers to sages, it becomes a little more ordinary and a little less all-powerful.
fear.practice: Name your fear out loud, the way Montaigne named his: “Right now I’m afraid because…” — and add: “as soldiers and sages have been too.” Notice whether things feel a little roomier.

sadness.text: “I do not portray being: I portray passing,” Montaigne wrote of his book, and the phrase suits sadness better than any consolation. Sadness came without asking, and right now it colours everything. Montaigne, though, spoke of it without pathos: he admitted that he himself was not very prone to sorrow and saw no reason to honour it as a virtue, even though people often dress it up in wisdom and importance. This is a freeing thought: sadness doesn’t have to be deep, significant or “earned.” It needs neither to be glorified nor defeated — it is enough not to let it become your final face. Montaigne believed we never stay the same for longer than an hour: mood, health and weather change us constantly. So sadness, too, is not a verdict but one of the soul’s weathers, which has come and will go in its own time.
sadness.practice: Go to a window and find weather out there that resembles your sadness: drizzle, fog, a low sky. Name it — and notice that a minute later the sky is already a little different.

grief.text: Eighteen years after the death of his friend Étienne de La Boétie, travelling in Italy, Montaigne noted in his journal that he had spent the whole day in painful thoughts of him. Grief does not keep to a calendar, and yours doesn’t either. That death was the great loss of his life, and years later he wrote that without him he lived only “by halves.” In “Of Diversion” he admits that reasoned consolations almost never work on grief head-on. What helps is rather time, a change of scene, a gentle shift of attention — not in order to forget, but to give the heart a breathing space. Many believe the Essays themselves grew out of this loss: having no one left to talk to, Montaigne began to talk to paper. Your grief, too, may one day become a conversation that goes on.
grief.practice: If you feel like it, write a line or two to the person you’ve lost, the way Montaigne went on talking to La Boétie on paper: what you noticed today and would have liked to share.

loneliness.text: Montaigne had sayings painted on his library’s ceiling beams, so that looking up from a book he always met a companion. Loneliness hurts, and he knew it: he lost the fullest friendship of his life early. He treasured friendship and solitude alike. He drew a fine distinction between them: in the essay “Of Solitude” he advises keeping for yourself a “back room” of the soul, where you can be yourself and converse with yourself. But this is solitude you choose, not solitude imposed on you. Montaigne named three kinds of company that nourished him: friendship, love and books. Books, he wrote, are always at hand and don’t mind being turned to only when there is no other company. To carry his thought further: until real closeness comes, you are not entirely alone — you have a companion within, and the voices of those who wrote before you.
loneliness.practice: Open a book that’s dear to you and read one page as if the author were speaking to you personally — like Montaigne looking up at his beams.

anger.text: Montaigne would ask your anger a simple question: who is speaking right now — you, or your passion? The anger didn’t flare up out of nowhere: something important has been touched. Montaigne wrote an essay “Of Anger” and was candid in it: he himself was quick-tempered, especially over small things. His observations are remarkably practical. He advised not to punish or decide anything until anger has cooled: in anger, he wrote, it is passion that speaks, not we ourselves. At the same time, he didn’t urge driving anger inward — anger held in, he said, eats away at us more than anger expressed briefly and moderately. Montaigne preferred a flare-up that quickly dies down to smouldering resentment. This view lets you acknowledge anger, not be ashamed of it, and still give it a little time before you act.
anger.practice: Before you reply or decide anything, go for a short walk — or at least pace the room while it is the passion speaking, not you. The decision can wait until tomorrow.

shame.text: “This is a book of good faith, reader,” Montaigne begins the Essays, where he tells everything about himself, down to his poor memory and his kidney stones. Shame pulls the other way: to hide, to become invisible. Montaigne did almost the opposite. In his note “To the Reader” he says he would gladly have portrayed himself whole and naked, had custom allowed it. In the later essays he writes calmly about illnesses, a poor memory, bodily habits — things people usually keep quiet about. His main argument: all of this we share with everyone, king or philosopher. For Montaigne, shame loses some of its power when we remember that our “shameful” weakness is simply human. There’s no need to put it on display, but you can stop thinking of it as a brand that only you bear.
shame.practice: Imagine your shame as a line in the Essays — one calm sentence, the way Montaigne spoke of his kidney stones. Say it to yourself and ask: how many people could have that same line?

guilt.text: “Others form man; I tell of him,” Montaigne begins the essay “Of Repentance.” The guilt you feel says that you care how your actions have affected others. In that essay he thought about guilt in an unusual way. He distinguished real repentance, which changes what we do, from the habit of endlessly punishing ourselves without changing anything. Montaigne admitted that he rarely repented — and not out of smugness: he felt he had been what he could be in those circumstances, and that a soul turned toward amendment matters more than a soul that only groans. You can take this as a support: guilt is useful when it tells you what to put right or whom to ask for forgiveness. When it turns into a constant trial of yourself, Montaigne would gently remind you that you are not only this one act.
guilt.practice: Pick one small thing you can put right or say today — an apology, a message, returning something — and do it. Let the rest wait for now.

envy.text: “Even on the highest throne in the world, we are still sitting only on our own bottom,” Montaigne reminds us, and it may be the best inoculation against envy. It can still sting: we are always comparing. Montaigne noticed that we rarely see another person’s life whole — only its façade, its best side. In the late essays he wrote that people seek other conditions because they don’t know how to use their own, and go outside themselves because they don’t know what is within. Montaigne also believed that each person bears the entire form of the human condition. Following Montaigne, to envy is to forget that your own life, with all its imperfections, is a complete example of a human life.
envy.practice: Swap places in your mind with the person you envy — entirely: their body, their past, their sleepless nights and worries, not just the façade. Would you agree? What of your own would you never give up?

emptiness.text: What does the mind do when it has nothing to do? Montaigne tested this on himself. If right now you want nothing and everything seems to have lost its taste, his answer may come in handy. In the essay “Of Idleness” he tells how, having withdrawn from public affairs, he hoped for peace, but his mind, left with nothing to do, became like a runaway horse: it bred vague chimeras one after another. The way out he found was modest — he began writing down what he saw in himself, with no plan or aim. That is how the Essays came about: “essais,” that is, “tries,” “attempts.” For Montaigne, emptiness doesn’t have to be filled with some great meaning. Sometimes a small attempt to notice something and write it down is enough — and life slowly begins to regain its taste.
emptiness.practice: Find one small impression today for each sense: a sound, a smell, a taste, a touch. Stay with each for a couple of breaths — this is your small “essay,” your trial.

confusion.text: Montaigne kept revising his book until his death, writing new thoughts in the margins that sometimes argued with the old ones. If the familiar answers have stopped working for you right now, for him that was almost the normal state of the mind. His motto was the question “What do I know?”, and in his longest essay, the “Apology for Raymond Sebond,” he shows how little we know for certain: the opinions of nations contradict each other, our senses deceive us, and our judgements shift along with our mood and health. Montaigne’s scepticism is not desperate but calm, even cheerful. If no one knows everything, then you don’t have to have a clear answer right now either. You can allow yourself not to know, to keep asking and trying — after all, Montaigne himself spent his whole life writing “attempts,” not final truths.
confusion.practice: Say the question that has you tangled out loud and add, as Montaigne did: “What do I know?” — and then: “For now I don’t know, and that’s allowed.” Notice whether anything has changed in your body.

quote.author: Michel de Montaigne
quote.source: Essays, Book II, ch. 12, “Apology for Raymond Sebond”

fatigue.text: Montaigne was not ashamed to admit that sleep had taken up a large part of his life. Your tiredness, too, is the honest voice of the body, and it’s worth listening to. Montaigne wrote a great deal about his body: about illness, about sleep, about how his mind changed when he was tired or unwell. He didn’t consider this lower than “lofty” thought. He was once elected mayor of Bordeaux, and he wrote that he was ready to take the business in hand but would not let it get “into his liver”: the mayor and Montaigne were always two different people. This boundary feels very modern. For Montaigne, you can do your work conscientiously without giving all of yourself to it. Tiredness may be a signal that a role has taken up too much room, and the person has been left without rest.
fatigue.practice: Take off your role for half an hour, the way Montaigne left the mayor at the door: put one work thing out of sight — the laptop, the work chat, the badge — and do something that belongs to you alone.

boredom.text: “When I play with my cat, who knows whether she is not amusing herself with me more than I with her?” Montaigne asked. Boredom seems trivial but is hard to bear, and he could find an interesting subject even in a cat, and in himself. He warned the reader that he himself was the matter of his book, and this subject turned out to be inexhaustible: thoughts, habits, contradictions, changes of mood. Montaigne also thought a great deal about what makes time alive. In the late essays he says that when the time is bad he “passes” it, and when it is good he doesn’t want to pass it but savours it. For Montaigne, boredom is an invitation not to hurry time along but to look more closely: what is going on in me right now, if the outside world is offering nothing?
boredom.practice: Watch yourself for a minute, the way Montaigne watched his cat: what are your hands doing, where does your gaze go, what thought just ran past? Let one small thing surprise you.

joy.text: “When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep,” Montaigne writes in his last essay, and that seems to be his whole recipe for joy. He valued it very highly and defended it against gloomy moralists. He held that knowing how to truly enjoy one’s own being is an almost divine perfection. In the essay “Of Experience” he writes that life is a gift to be received with gratitude, rejecting neither the joys of the body nor those of the soul. He did not despise pleasures, but he liked to taste them slowly and attentively. He admitted: the shorter life is, the more deeply and fully he wanted to live it. For Montaigne, joy is nothing to be ashamed of, it needs no justification, and it will not be “punished” by troubles to come. It is worth simply noticing it and letting it stay a while.
joy.practice: Do what is making you glad, and only that — like Montaigne when he danced. Three slow breaths, “right now it’s good” — and add nothing more.

love.text: “Because it was he, because it was I” — that is all Montaigne could ever say about why he loved his friend. The tenderness you feel now is made of the same stuff. Montaigne knew love above all as friendship: his friendship with Étienne de La Boétie was so complete that he wrote of two souls blending so thoroughly that the seam joining them could no longer be found. There is something comforting in this: love needs no justification; you don’t have to earn it with a list of qualities. Montaigne was reserved about passion, calling it a rash and fickle fire, but he placed tenderness grounded in closeness very high. Allow yourself simply to love, without demanding that the feeling explain itself.
love.practice: Tell someone you love one thing you love about them today — without explaining why. “Because it’s you” is reason enough.

quote.text: Because it was he, because it was I.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne

gratitude.text: Montaigne’s father had his son woken in the mornings by music, so as not to startle the child with an abrupt awakening — and the son remembered it all his life. The gratitude you feel now makes life warmer, and Montaigne knew how to keep its reasons in mind. He wrote lovingly of his father, who tried to bring him up gently. All his life he returned with gratitude to his four years of friendship with La Boétie. And in the last essay he says that he loves life and accepts it as it has been given. For Montaigne, gratitude is the ability to see your ordinary life as a gift, not only as a list of what’s missing.
gratitude.practice: Think of someone who once did something gentle and unnoticed for you, like that morning music — and if you can, tell them today, in a message or a call.

hope.text: Montaigne the sceptic distrusted predictions — gloomy and rosy alike — and out of that distrust, oddly enough, grew the sturdiest kind of hope. You need it to keep going when the present is hard. Montaigne was cautious about it: he noticed that hopes, like fears, carry us off into the future, and because of them we miss the life that is happening now. But his scepticism works in the other direction too. If we know the future so poorly, then gloomy predictions can’t be final either. Montaigne saw how quickly people, circumstances, even his own judgements changed. The best hope in Montaigne is not a dream of something far off but trust in the changeability of life. Since everything changes, your present situation isn’t forever either.
hope.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, out loud — the story of a time things turned out unexpectedly well. Montaigne collected such cases as proof that no one knows the future.

nostalgia.text: Little Montaigne’s first language was Latin: his father surrounded him with servants and tutors who spoke only Latin to the child. The past stays in us just as firmly, and right now you seem to feel a tenderness for it with a bittersweet edge. Montaigne, who began writing the Essays in his mature years, often recalled his youth, his friend, his father, old joys. But he regarded the past calmly: in “Of Repentance” he says that if he had to live his life over again, he would live it just as he had. This is not boasting but acceptance: each age has its own joys, and old age need not envy youth. In Montaigne, nostalgia can enrich rather than torment. The past remains yours; it made you who you are now, and you can draw warmth from it without demanding that it come back.
nostalgia.practice: Recall one warm moment from the past in full detail — sound, light, smell. Then ask yourself: what of this do I carry with me today?

craving.text: What happens if you simply watch a wave without arguing with it? Montaigne tested this on his own impulses. Right now your whole body may be saying “now, right away” — that is a powerful wave, not a verdict on your character. Montaigne wrote a lot about how our desire grows stronger with obstacles and prohibitions: the more we argue with a desire, the louder it gets. His method was different — observing himself without judgement. He examined his impulses with interest, like weather, and noticed that they don’t stay the same: everything in a human being, he wrote, is in constant motion. So a craving, too, shifts from place to place, rises and subsides. You can choose not to fight it but simply to watch the wave rise and then, like any wave, begin to fall.
craving.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and watch the craving the way Montaigne watched his impulses: where is it in your body, is it growing, is it changing? Don’t do anything — just notice.

addiction.text: Montaigne retells the story of a woman who carried a calf in her arms every day and went on carrying it when it had grown into an ox — she never noticed the burden becoming impossible. Addiction works in a similar way: not a moral failure but a cycle that grows very strong over time. In his essay on custom he calls it an imperious and treacherous schoolmistress: at first she establishes her authority quietly and unnoticed, and then she shows us a face we can hardly even raise our eyes to. Montaigne spoke of this not with contempt but with wonder at how habit reshapes both body and perception. Hence an important thought: what seems to be “my nature” often turns out to be simply a deeply rooted habit. A habit took shape gradually — and just as gradually, in small steps, it can be reshaped, especially not alone.
addiction.practice: Recall what this habit was like while it was still a “calf,” and what it gave you then. If you like, think about whom you could talk to about it calmly — for example, a mutual-help group of people who have walked a similar path.

hangover.text: Montaigne admitted that his memory was monstrously bad, and wrote about it with a smile rather than horror. The morning after can be hard: the body feels awful, and the head is full of anxiety, shame and fragments of memory. Montaigne wrote about drunkenness plainly and without romance, considering it a coarse vice that weakens judgement, but he didn’t make monsters of those who drink either. He wrote about his mistakes calmly, without self-flagellation. His advice would be simple: don’t fill the gaps with the worst guesses. The imagination, as he knew, inflates fears. It’s better to return to what you can know for certain, take care of your body, and give yourself time before passing sentence on yourself.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, in small sips, and name to yourself three things about last night that you know for certain. Let the rest stay a question for now, not a verdict.

euphoria.text: If Montaigne were beside you, he wouldn’t spoil this evening — he would only ask you to remember it properly. When everything seems possible, that flash is bright and real. He relished good moments and advised savouring them rather than rushing past. But he was also an attentive observer of his own changes. In the essay “Of the Inconsistency of Our Actions” he writes that we are all made of motley patches, each of which plays its own game. Euphoria is one of those patches: bright, real, but not the only one. You can live it fully and still remember that it is one of your states, not the final one. That makes it easier not to take big decisions only on its crest.
euphoria.practice: Write yourself a short note “in the margins,” as Montaigne did: what you feel and dream of right now — to reread in a few days, before deciding anything.

crash.text: Montaigne noticed that the same passage in a book could strike him one day as brilliant and another as empty — depending on how he had slept and what was aching. Perhaps that is how your whole life looks right now: what glowed yesterday looks grey today. He noticed that a healthy person and a sick one, a rested person and a tired one, see the very same things quite differently. In the “Apology for Raymond Sebond” he shows how unreliable our view is when we feel bad. For Montaigne, the comedown is not the truth about life finally revealed, but just another angle of vision, and a temporary one. Montaigne didn’t demand constancy of himself and didn’t think he was obliged to stay at the peak. You can simply wait it out, take care of yourself, and draw no conclusions about life as a whole.
crash.practice: Take care of your body today, the way Montaigne looked after his after an attack: a warm shower, a short nap, an unhurried walk. And put off big conclusions about life until a day when you feel steadier.

panic.text: “I am one of those who feel the power of imagination very strongly,” Montaigne admitted, and he knew how quickly it can set the heart pounding. If right now your heart is racing, your breathing falters and it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen, you are not alone in this. In the essay “Of Fear” Montaigne described what was called “panic terror”: a sudden fear that seizes people for no visible reason, when even the brave lose their heads. He saw in it not disgrace but a shared human vulnerability. In “Of the Power of the Imagination” he writes how strongly it acts on the body. Such waves usually peak and subside within a few minutes. You can return to the simplest things — to your body and what is around you, just as he brought his thoughts back to his walk in the garden.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and take a long exhale, longer than the inhale. Then, as Montaigne brought his thoughts back to the garden, bring your attention back to the room: name out loud five objects around you and their colour.

dread.text: Montaigne worked beneath a ceiling covered with sayings about human frailty — and yet he called simply living his trade and his art. The question “what is it all for?”, with an abyss suddenly opening behind it, was one he knew first-hand. In the early essays, following Cicero, he wrote that to philosophize is to learn to die. But for him the point of this thought was not gloom but liberation: whoever calmly accepts their finitude stops being afraid and can live more freely. And in the late essays Montaigne softened even further. He wrote that we spoil life by worrying about death, and that life should be its own aim. In Montaigne, finitude does not cancel meaning — it makes each ordinary day precious and real.
dread.practice: Do one simple thing now as if it were your trade and your art: make tea, water a plant, make the bed. Without any “what for” — just do it well.

fomo.text: “I have done nothing today,” we complain, and Montaigne replies: “What? Have you not lived? That is not only the fundamental but the most illustrious of your occupations.” When it feels as if life is happening somewhere else, to other people, those words are worth keeping close. Montaigne described this feeling long before social media: we are almost never at home in ourselves, he wrote — our thoughts are always somewhere further on. We chase after fame and other people’s opinion, forgetting about life here. For Montaigne, the most interesting place is where you are, if you are truly present there. Someone else’s party looks brighter because you see only its façade, while your own life reveals itself only from the inside.
fomo.practice: Put your phone down and look around: name three things happening right here that no one but you is seeing right now. That is what a day lived looks like.

sleepless.text: Who is talking to you at three in the morning — you, or a runaway horse? That is how Montaigne described a mind left with nothing to do. A sleepless night is hard: thoughts go round and round, and everything seems scarier than by day. In the essay “Of Idleness” that horse produces one absurd chimera after another. Montaigne decided to write these offspring of his mind down so that in time, as he joked, he might make it ashamed of them. There is a gentle wisdom here: night thoughts shouldn’t be taken for truth. They are the chimeras of an idle mind, not prophecies. You can put them down on paper and leave them until morning, when you can look at them more calmly.
sleepless.practice: Keep paper by your bed. Write the circling thoughts down in a single line — these are your “chimeras” — and tell yourself: “I’ll look at this in the morning.”

betrayal.text: Montaigne kept the gates of his château open even at the height of civil war: he reasoned that a house which doesn’t defend itself is less often a target. Betrayal wounds all the more deeply the more you trusted, and he trusted openly. It was the age of the Wars of Religion, when neighbours and even relatives became enemies. In “Of Friendship” he distinguishes perfect friendship, like his with La Boétie, from ordinary friendship, in which it is wise to keep a certain caution. This is not cynicism but sobriety: most bonds between people are imperfect, and not everyone is capable of what we invest in them. For Montaigne, betrayal says more about the other person’s limits than about your worth. Your capacity to trust is not a mistake but a virtue.
betrayal.practice: Say two sentences out loud: “What this says about them is…” and “What it doesn’t say about me is…”. Listen to how the second one sounds.

jealousy.text: In an essay with the harmless title “On Some Verses of Virgil,” Montaigne suddenly starts talking about jealousy — and calls it one of the most barren and restless maladies of the soul. If you are jealous now, love, fear of loss and pictures painted by the imagination are all mixed together in you. He noticed that jealousy feeds not so much on facts as on the imagination, which paints things that may never have happened. Montaigne didn’t condemn the jealous, but he saw how the feeling torments, above all, the person who feels it. Jealousy is a sign that the person is dear to you. But the pictures it paints are worth distinguishing from what you actually know. That boundary brings a little peace.
jealousy.practice: Write two columns: “what I know for certain” and “what I imagine.” Just look at which one is longer.

resentment.text: Montaigne had a “back room” of the soul — an inner space no one entered uninvited. An old grievance is like a lodger who moved in there without asking and won’t leave. Montaigne wrote in “Of Anger” that irritation held in eats away at us more than what is expressed and let go. He admitted that he preferred a brief flare-up to hidden rancour. Montaigne also valued freedom of judgement highly: in “Of Solitude” he advises freeing ourselves from whatever keeps us on a leash, so that the soul belongs to itself. Resentment keeps binding you to the person who hurt you, and gives them a place in that room. Acknowledging that it hurt, and gradually taking that space back for yourself, does not mean excusing the other person.
resentment.practice: Picture your “back room” and the person who has settled in it. Say to yourself, “It hurt,” and in your mind open the door for them to leave. Not forgiving — just taking the room back.

heartbreak.text: What heals the heart when the right words don’t help? Montaigne answered without embarrassment: a change of air. It probably hurts a great deal right now — one of the sharpest pains a human being knows. In “Of Diversion” he tells how he himself once coped with a heavy sorrow: not by reasoning, but by change — new impressions, occupations, people. He believed that the soul, like the body, is sometimes healed by time and a change of scene. This doesn’t mean feelings should be suppressed or that you should hurry to forget. Rather, it means giving yourself the right to a breathing space, to small joys alongside the grief. The heart, like everything in a person, is in motion — and that motion goes on.
heartbreak.practice: Pick one small change for today: a different route, a new song, a call to an old acquaintance. Not as a cure — just as a change of air.

impostor.text: Montaigne opened his book with a warning: “I myself am the matter of my book” — he promised the reader nothing grander. If you are haunted by the feeling that “any moment now they’ll find me out,” he could be a good antidote. He wrote openly about his weaknesses: a poor memory, a lack of learning, uncertainty in his judgements — and yet his book has been read for four centuries. No one is the majestic image they present on the outside. For Montaigne, being “exposed” would reveal nothing terrible: behind every façade there is an ordinary person with their own doubts. You are not a fraud — you simply see yourself from the inside and others from the outside.
impostor.practice: Imagine you’ve been “found out” and finish the sentence: “It would turn out that I…”. Consider whether it doesn’t describe anyone you respect.

self_hatred.text: “Each man bears the entire form of the human condition,” Montaigne wrote, and that includes you on your very worst day. Your inner critic is merciless right now, and it is hard to listen to. Montaigne, for all his strictness about his own flaws, considered self-hatred unnatural. He wrote that the highest, almost divine perfection is knowing how to enjoy one’s own being rightly. He devoted his whole book to observing himself without a verdict: with curiosity, irony, and acceptance that he was as he was. So the voice that says you are worse than others is simply mistaken: you are as much an example of human life as anyone else. This is something you can come to accept gradually, without hurrying.
self_hatred.practice: Say one of your inner critic’s phrases out loud — then answer it the way La Boétie would have answered Montaigne: kindly, but honestly.

helplessness.text: In the summer of 1585, when plague broke out around his home, Montaigne spent six months leading his family from house to house in search of shelter — he called himself the guide of this caravan. When circumstances are stronger than you, it is genuinely hard, and he knew it. Wars of Religion, plague, serious illness — he didn’t pretend that everything depended on him. But he made a distinction: what can I influence — and what lies beyond my will? Even as mayor of Bordeaux he tried to do his job honestly without taking on the whole weight of the world. Even when we can’t change the course of events, we still have how we meet them, and the small things that are still in our hands.
helplessness.practice: Choose one very small thing you can do today — the way the guide of a caravan picks the next stop, not the whole route. Then do it.

procrastination.text: The French “essai,” which gave its name to a whole genre, simply means “attempt,” “trial”: Montaigne gave his book that name so that no one would expect perfection from it. When you can’t get started, the task usually seems too big, or bound to come out perfect. He wrote without a plan, in fragments, returning to thoughts, contradicting himself, and he kept adding to his book for years, layer upon layer. He didn’t wait until everything was clear — he tried. You don’t need to create a finished thing straight away. First you just need an attempt, a draft, an awkward first line. Montaigne might say that the most interesting part begins exactly where you allow yourself to try imperfectly.
procrastination.practice: Call the task you’re putting off an “attempt” and do the smallest version of it — for example, one line or five minutes of work.

uprooted.text: In Italy Montaigne was so taken with the place that he kept part of his travel journal in Italian, and in Rome he obtained the title of Roman citizen. Moving, emigrating, losing the ground under your feet is a deep experience, even if the new place has joys of its own. Montaigne travelled a great deal, through Germany, Switzerland and Italy, and later, because of a plague epidemic, he was forced to leave his home. In the essay “Of Vanity” he wrote that he regarded all people as his compatriots. In “Of Cannibals” he observed that everyone calls barbarism whatever is not their own custom. Being torn from home is painful, but it is also a chance to see that many familiar things were only custom. Montaigne’s home was also within — in that “back room” of the soul that you can carry with you anywhere.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place the way Montaigne walked around Italy — with a question rather than a verdict. Find one local detail you already like in some way, and one habit of your own that you brought with you.

overload.text: On his thirty-eighth birthday Montaigne had an inscription painted on the wall of his study: he was retiring “to the bosom of the learned Muses,” where it is quiet. When there is too much information, too many people and demands around you, that quiet starts to feel like a luxury. Montaigne, who lived in an age of wars and pamphlets, left advice that sounds surprisingly modern. In “Of Solitude” he proposes keeping for ourselves a “back room,” entirely our own, where we can be free and converse with ourselves. This corner doesn’t require giving up the world; it only shields the mind from the noise. In the late essays Montaigne describes how, walking in his garden, he brings his wandering thoughts back to the walk itself, to the garden, to himself. Overload is a sign that your “back room” is short of quiet.
overload.practice: Set aside five minutes without screens. Sit by a window or take a short walk, and keep bringing your thoughts back to what you see and feel right now, like Montaigne in his garden.

unreality.text: “Perhaps we sleep while waking and wake while sleeping,” Montaigne cautiously suggested, retelling the ancients. When everything around you feels unreal, it is strange and unsettling — but people were thinking about it long before you. Montaigne reflected on this in the “Apology for Raymond Sebond.” He admitted that our senses often deceive us and that we have no direct communication with being — we see the world through our own shifting perceptions. But for Montaigne this was no cause for panic: every human being is made this way. Your experience doesn’t make you strange; it is one facet of the shared fragility of perception. You can gently keep returning to simple sensations — your body, a sound, something solid to lean on.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a noticeable texture — fabric, wood, stone. Describe it out loud: is it warm or cold, smooth or rough?

awe.text: “This great world is the mirror in which we must look at ourselves to know ourselves rightly,” Montaigne wrote. The awe you feel is rare and precious, and he felt it before the diversity of the world. In the “Apology for Raymond Sebond” he speaks with wonder of the sky and the stars, of animals and the customs of distant peoples, of how little a human being understands of the universe. For Montaigne this sense of smallness doesn’t crush — it frees: it teaches modesty and curiosity. Awe is a moment when you see the world at its true scale, and you can simply let yourself marvel at it. Montaigne was in no hurry to explain such moments — he let them last.
awe.practice: Let your gaze rest on whatever filled you with awe for one more minute — as into the mirror Montaigne wrote about. Don’t take a photo, just look.

relief.text: Montaigne, who suffered from kidney stones for years, insisted that there is no pleasure brighter than the moment an attack lets go. Now the weight has lifted, and a warm wave is moving through you. In the late essays he describes that moment with evident delight. He noticed that health after pain feels especially bright and delicious. Montaigne advised not to rush past such moments: he wrote that good time is not something you want to “pass” but something you want to savour. For Montaigne, relief is not just the absence of something bad but a joy in its own right, worth noticing and living fully. There’s no need to move straight on to the next worry — you can give yourself time to enjoy the fact that things have become lighter.
relief.practice: Take a deep breath in and a slow breath out. Tell yourself, “It’s easier now,” — and stay with that feeling for another minute, savouring it, as Montaigne did.

calm.text: “When I walk alone in a beautiful orchard, if my thoughts have been dwelling on other things, I bring them back to the walk, to the orchard, to myself,” Montaigne writes. The calm you feel now is precious, and he knew how to value it. This is from “Of Experience,” and it is about simple presence. He believed that the chief art is to live: not in a hurry, not for the sake of the future, but now. For him, calm is neither emptiness nor inaction but full presence in what you are doing. Good time, he wrote, is not something to “pass” but something to savour. You needn’t rush to analyse this state — you can simply go on being in it.
calm.practice: For a minute or two, do nothing: just sit, like Montaigne in his orchard, and when your thoughts run off, gently bring them back — to the chair, to your breath, to yourself.

quote.text: When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne

inspiration.text: “My thoughts fall asleep if I make them sit down,” Montaigne admitted, and so he did his thinking on foot and on horseback. Right now thoughts are coming freely and you want to act — the moment not to scare them away. He wrote his book not to a plan but by following his thought, letting it branch, return, contradict itself. He admitted that his style and his mind wander “by leaps and gambols,” and saw no harm in it. He kept adding to the Essays for years, right in the margins. Inspiration doesn’t need to be forced into a strict scheme. You can simply catch it — write it down as it is and put it in order later. Montaigne showed that a living thought, honestly written down, is worth more than a polished but lifeless one.
inspiration.practice: Go for a walk, as Montaigne did, and let the thought lead. When you come back, sketch out what came, as it is, unedited — you can put it in order later.

schadenfreude.text: In ancient Athens, Montaigne tells us, a seller of funeral goods was condemned for profiting from other people’s deaths — and then Montaigne turns the mirror on the reader. The schadenfreude you’ve noticed in yourself is awkward, but he wouldn’t judge you: each of us has things inside we don’t like to admit. This is from the short essay “One Man’s Profit Is Another Man’s Harm,” and its conclusion is honest: if each of us looks within, we will find that most of our secret wishes are born and nourished at someone else’s expense. Montaigne pronounces no verdict on this — he simply describes human nature as it is. Schadenfreude doesn’t make you a monster; it makes you human. What matters is only what you do next: to notice the feeling and not turn it into words or actions that hurt someone.
schadenfreude.practice: Note to yourself: “There it is — the very feeling Montaigne wrote about.” Ask: what am I missing right now, if someone else’s failure is so comforting?

contempt.text: In Rouen Montaigne asked the Brazilian natives brought to the king what had surprised them most in France — and recorded answers that would embarrass any Frenchman. Contempt gives a pleasant sense of being right, and he spent his whole life testing such feelings. In “Of Cannibals” he writes that everyone calls barbarism whatever is not their own custom. Our standards, Montaigne believed, are largely a product of habit, place and upbringing, and so to despise others on their basis is to judge another life by your own rulebook. He could be mocking too — he admitted that Democritus laughing at human folly was closer to him than Heraclitus weeping over it — but he most readily turned that mocking gaze on himself. Contempt often protects us from something unpleasant or frightening. Montaigne would ask, with curiosity: what yardstick am I measuring by right now, and where did I get it?
contempt.practice: Look at the person you despise through the eyes of those visitors in Rouen: in what place or setting would their behaviour be the norm? You don’t have to agree — just try on a different yardstick.

disgust.text: Montaigne wrote a whole little essay “Of Smells” and admitted that his moustache kept a scent all day long. Disgust arrives just as fast — a strong, almost instantaneous feeling. In the essay “Of Custom” he gathers many examples of things that are revolting to one people and perfectly natural to another, and concludes: custom dulls our senses and quietly shapes our judgements, passing them off as laws of nature. This doesn’t mean your disgust is false — the body knows what it needs to pull away from. But it helps to remember that part of disgust is learned. This applies to disgust with yourself as well: Montaigne wrote without embarrassment about his body, its illnesses and habits, believing all of it to be the common human lot. Look at your disgust as a researcher would: how much of it comes from the body, and how much from habit?
disgust.practice: Ask yourself, like a researcher: when did I first learn that this was “disgusting,” and from whom? If someone close is nearby, ask them too — your answers may turn out to differ.

revenge.text: The emperor Augustus, Montaigne tells us, on learning of Cinna’s conspiracy, spent an agonizing night deciding whether to take revenge. Your wish for revenge is also born of pain that seeks an outlet and seeks justice. In the essay “Cowardice, the Mother of Cruelty” he observes that cruelty is often born not of strength but of weakness and fear. Augustus, in the end, on his wife’s advice, pardoned the conspirator — and, as Montaigne writes, no one ever plotted against him again. Montaigne offers this not as a lesson in piety but as an example of how unpredictable the outcomes of our decisions are. There may be a hint here for you: the wish for revenge is a signal of a deep wound, and it matters to acknowledge it. And the decision about what to do with it is better made once the storm has settled.
revenge.practice: Postpone any decision connected with the hurt for at least a day — like Augustus, who listened to his wife first. Tell someone you trust what you really want from the situation: acknowledgement, an apology, safety?

anger_at_loved.text: Why do those closest to us irritate us more than strangers? Montaigne found the answer in his own household. This anger is especially tormenting, because shame follows close behind. He admitted that what vexed him most was not great misfortunes but the small everyday frictions of domestic life — exactly where people live side by side. We have the most of these small things with those close to us, and they pile up. Montaigne firmly opposed strictness and violence in raising children and wanted to be loved rather than feared. But he didn’t demand angelic patience of himself: a human being, he was convinced, is changeable, and tenderness and irritation live perfectly well together in one heart. Anger at someone close doesn’t disprove love. It says that you are tired, that something keeps repeating — and that this is worth talking about in a calm moment.
anger_at_loved.practice: Find the “splinter” — the recurring small thing behind the last flare-up — and in a calm moment suggest to the person that you talk about that, not about the flare-up.

ambivalence.text: “We Taste Nothing Pure” is the title of one of Montaigne’s essays. If you love someone and at the same time can’t stand them, that is not a sign of falseness but, according to Montaigne, an ordinary feature of our nature. In “Of the Inconsistency of Our Actions” he writes that we are all made of patches, and each patch plays its own part at every moment. And in the essay with that very title he shows that none of our pleasures is ever unmixed: there is always a drop of bitterness in it. Mixed feelings toward someone close are not a mistake to be fixed by choosing the “right” feeling. They are an honest picture of your bond. Montaigne didn’t aim for neatness; he aimed for truthfulness. Allow yourself, too, to be inconsistent in your feelings — and to look at this with interest rather than fear.
ambivalence.practice: Say two sentences to yourself: “What I love in you is…” and “What drives me up the wall is…” — and don’t choose between them. Both patches are yours.

quote.text: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne
quote.source: Essays, Book II, ch. 1, “Of the Inconsistency of Our Actions”

guilty_relief.text: Montaigne titled one of his essays “How We Cry and Laugh for the Same Thing” — and filled it with people who grieved and felt relief at once. Relief you feel ashamed of is one of the most hidden feelings. He gives examples from history and from his own life and explains: many different feelings move in the soul at once, and now one, now another comes to the fore. We are not being hypocrites when we weep and at the same time feel relief; the soul looks at one event with different eyes. Relief after a loved one’s departure, a breakup, or a long illness does not cancel your love and grief. It speaks of the weight you were carrying. Montaigne, who always preferred the truth about himself to a fine pose, would say: both feelings are true, and neither needs to be hidden from yourself.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your palm on your chest and tell yourself: “Different feelings are moving in me right now, and all of them are real.” Name each one in a single word.

indifference.text: The captive Egyptian king Psammenitus watched in silence as his children were led past him — and wept only on seeing one of his companions; Montaigne took this story as a key to puzzling numbness. If an event “ought” to move you, yet inside there is silence, that is unsettling — but perhaps emptiness is not the point. Montaigne was candid: in the essay “Of Sadness” he admits that he himself is little subject to this passion. Montaigne explains: the soul was filled to the brim, and the last drop broke the dam. Outward calm is not the same as unfeeling. Sometimes feelings are too big, or we are too tired, and they come later, at an unexpected moment. Don’t force yourself to act out what isn’t there right now. Montaigne trusted his changeable nature — you can trust yours too.
indifference.practice: Instead of checking yourself for the “right” feelings, rest your hands on your knees and for a minute simply notice your body: heaviness, lightness, tiredness. That is enough.

escape.text: “You took yourself along,” Socrates told a man whom travel hadn’t helped; Montaigne loved this story, though he himself adored the road. He, too, knew the dream of dropping everything and going away. At thirty-eight he left his post in the Parlement of Bordeaux and withdrew to his tower with its library to read and think. Later he travelled for a long time and admitted that he loved the road. But in the essay “Of Solitude” he passes on Socrates’ words as a warning. Montaigne concludes: it is not enough to get away from people and places; you have to free yourself from the cares and habits that sit inside. The wish to escape is a legitimate signal that you need space. The only question is what exactly you want to leave behind, and what to take with you.
escape.practice: Imagine you’ve already left, and unpack your suitcase: which inner habits did you most likely bring along? Choose one you could loosen right here.

forbidden_attraction.text: Montaigne gave one of his essays a title that sounds like a diagnosis: “That Our Desire Is Increased by Difficulty.” Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and frightening. He gathered many examples of how prohibition, obstacles and unavailability inflame desire, while ease and permission cool it down. Montaigne looked at this without moralizing, with a researcher’s curiosity about human nature. To carry his thought further, part of the strength of your attraction may be born of the unavailability itself, not only of the person. This is neither a verdict on the feeling nor advice on what to do. It is a chance to see how desire works — and to understand what in it is truly yours: what thirst for life, attention or freedom is looking for an outlet here. Such understanding gives more freedom than either prohibition or blindly following the feeling.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Try a thought experiment in Montaigne’s spirit: imagine this person were available and everything were simple. What would be left of the feeling? Just notice the answer, without judging it.

social_anxiety.text: “The world always looks straight ahead; as for me, I turn my gaze inward,” Montaigne writes in “Of Presumption,” and there is an unexpected comfort in it for the shy. If every conversation is turning into an ordeal right now, this observation lowers the stakes. He liked to remind us that all people, however important they look, are made of the same stuff as you: each has a body, tiredness, weaknesses and funny habits. There is comfort, too, in this: the people around you are far more occupied with themselves than it seems, and watch you less than your anxiety suggests. Montaigne didn’t demand courage. He suggested being as natural as you can manage, and accepting your awkwardness as part of the same human face that everyone has.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next meeting, silently note one ordinary human detail in each person you talk to: tiredness, a little laugh, nervousness. You are among people just like you.

quote.text: And on the loftiest throne in the world we are still sitting only on our own rump.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne

uncertainty.text: Montaigne’s commemorative token bore a pair of scales with the pans in balance and the question “What do I know?”. When it’s unclear what will happen, you long so much for at least some certainty. Montaigne, a sceptic by conviction, lived with uncertainty as a constant companion — and learned to find peace in it. The scales are an image of what the ancient sceptics called suspension of judgement: not rushing to a verdict where there is no knowledge. In the essay “Of the Uncertainty of Our Judgement” he shows how often events turn out quite differently from what the wisest people predicted. Uncertainty is not a malfunction but the ordinary condition of human life. You don’t need to know the future to live today. You can hold the question open, like the scales, and get on with what is in front of you.
uncertainty.practice: Hold out both palms like the pans of a scale, and place one possible outcome on each. Leave them in balance and choose one thing to do today that makes sense whichever way it goes.

waiting.text: One of Montaigne’s early essays is called “Our Feelings Reach Out Beyond Us” — as if it were written about someone waiting for an answer. When you’re waiting, it feels as if life will begin only once the answer comes. He writes that we are never at home, we are always somewhere outside ourselves: fear, desire and hope push us toward the future and take away our ability to feel and consider what is here now. Montaigne doesn’t reproach us for it — such is our nature. But all his life he practised bringing his attention back to the present hour, to the simple pleasure of being. The waiting won’t disappear because of this, and the answer will come when it comes. But between “now” and “later” there is still living time, and it is yours too.
waiting.practice: For two minutes, simply name to yourself what you see, hear and feel in your body. This time is your life too, not a waiting room.

regret.text: What did you know then, and what could you do? Montaigne asked himself this before he would repent. Regret over what you did or didn’t do can hold on for a long time. In “Of Repentance” he took an unusual position. He distinguished errors of the will from unlucky outcomes. If a decision was made honestly, in the light of what he knew and could do at the time, and it turned out badly, that, for Montaigne, was a matter of fortune, not a cause for repentance: a decision should be judged by the circumstances of its time, not by its result. Montaigne didn’t call for complacency and was strict about genuinely bad deeds. But he suggested telling real guilt apart from regret that life didn’t turn out as you wished. The latter is not a crime but part of the human lot.
regret.practice: Take one regret and ask, Montaigne-style: what did I know then, and what could I do? Was this an error of my will, or the unlucky outcome of an honest decision? It’s enough to say the answer to yourself.

longing.text: “Friendship has arms long enough,” Montaigne replied to those who reproached him for his long absences from home. When you long for a particular person, it is heavy, but it is also a very living feeling: it tells you how much this bond means to you. In “Of Vanity” he goes on: those arms are long enough to hold on to each other from one end of the world to the other. Separation doesn’t break the bond. It makes it different — more inward and more conscious. Montaigne, who kept up an inner conversation with his closest friend for years, knew that the people we love remain part of our inner world. Longing is also a form of presence. You don’t have to drive it away; you can turn it into conversation.
longing.practice: Recall what you value most in this person, and today do one small thing in that spirit — the way they would have done it.

world_pain.text: Montaigne hated cruelty above all vices, and he could not even watch a chicken’s neck being wrung without distress. Hard news wounds those capable of compassion, and your pain for the world comes from the same source. Montaigne lived in a very hard time — for decades France was torn apart by civil wars, and in 1585 a plague epidemic forced him and his family to leave home. Yet Montaigne didn’t let the pain swallow him whole. In the essay “Of Physiognomy” he tells of the courage and calm with which the ordinary people around him bore the common misfortunes. He went on reading, writing, keeping up friendships and doing his duties — not out of indifference, but because life goes on even amid calamity. Compassion and ordinary life don’t contradict each other. Taking care of yourself is not a betrayal of those who are suffering.
world_pain.practice: Today, give the news a set amount of time and close it afterwards. Then do one ordinary thing — a walk, a meal, a phone call — fully, with attention.

rejection.text: Books, Montaigne wrote, always greet him “with the same face,” whatever mood he comes to them in. Rejection hurts: it feels as if you have been assessed and found wanting. Montaigne looked for a support that doesn’t depend on someone else’s “yes” or “no.” In the essay “Of Solitude” he advises keeping a “back room” for yourself — an inner space that belongs wholly to you, where you can talk with yourself and be with yourself. And in “Of Three Kinds of Association” he admits that books consoled him in every misfortune. Montaigne didn’t urge shutting yourself off from people — he valued friendship very highly. But he reminds us that your worth is not issued by others and cannot be revoked by them. Another person’s refusal speaks of their choice. Your inner dwelling stays with you.
rejection.practice: Name your “inner dwelling”: an activity, place or thought where you feel like yourself. Spend at least ten minutes there today.

quote.text: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne

abandonment.text: “We must lend ourselves to others and give ourselves only to ourselves,” Montaigne advised. The fear of being abandoned keeps you in constant tension, and he, having lost his closest friend, knew the price of attachment. In the essay “Of Solitude” he gives advice that sounds not cold but caring: we should have loved ones, a home, occupations, but not be so bound to them that all our happiness depends on them alone. This is not about loving less. It is about your life having several supports and a centre of its own — then love for a person doesn’t turn into a constant fear of losing the ground beneath your feet. The fear of abandonment can be met not only with checking and worry but also with care for yourself: for your interests, friends, pursuits. The sturdier your inner home, the more calmly you can love.
abandonment.practice: List five things that support you apart from this person: people, activities, places, habits. Choose one and give it some time today.

unrequited.text: Passion, Montaigne wrote, is like a feverish heat: it has its fits and its lulls. If your heart gives and nothing comes back, this pain, too, lives in waves. Montaigne wrote about love with striking precision. This is from “Of Friendship,” where he calls passion a rash and fickle fire. This is not a reproach to love but a portrait of it: such passion lives in waves. So the pain of unrequited love won’t always be the same either — it too will have its fits and its respites. Montaigne, sceptic and observer, would suggest watching these waves without hurry and without judgement. Your feeling speaks of your capacity to love warmly. There’s no need to be ashamed of it — and it does not oblige you to wait for an answer forever.
unrequited.practice: For several days in a row, rate on a scale of 1 to 10 how strong the pain is today. Watch how it changes — it has its own ebbs and flows.

humiliation.text: “The mayor and Montaigne have always been two, very clearly separated,” he wrote after two terms as mayor of Bordeaux. Humiliation burns: it feels as if you have been made smaller in front of everyone. He understood well the difference between the role and the person. You can play a role without merging with it. This thought helps with humiliation. What was struck was your image, your position, your role in someone’s eyes — and that is painful and unfair. But beneath the role there remains a person who cannot be demoted. Montaigne also believed that other people’s opinion depends largely on chance and mood, and advised against building the edifice of your worth on it. Let yourself feel the hurt — and remember that it touches the mask, not the face.
humiliation.practice: In your mind, take off the role that was struck, like a costume, and list to yourself what remained untouched beneath it: your values, your loved ones, your skills.

body_shame.text: “I am below average height,” Montaigne calmly informs us in “Of Presumption,” adding that this is inconvenient, especially when you have to give orders to others. Dissatisfaction with your body can be agonizing, and he understood that. He didn’t embellish his appearance, nor did he make a tragedy of it. And in “Of Physiognomy” he reflects on Socrates, whose outward appearance was said to be ugly — and whose soul was beautiful. Montaigne doesn’t deny that beauty is a power and a joy. But he shows that a person’s appearance and their worth are different things, and that you can live with the body you have without being at war with it. For Montaigne the body was not an adversary but a companion with whom he shared pleasures and ailments. You can come to terms with it.
body_shame.practice: Say two or three sentences about yourself out loud, the way Montaigne might: honestly, calmly, with a touch of humour — without praise and without reproach.

illness.text: Montaigne was sure he had inherited his kidney stones from his father — a legacy he wrote about with wry irony. When your body lets you down, the world narrows to pain and limitations, and he knew this first-hand. In the second half of his life he wrote many honest pages about his illness. But he learned to hold something like a conversation with the illness: to notice the respites between attacks, to take pleasure in ordinary things when it let up, and not to hand his whole life over to the ailment in advance. In “Of Experience” he writes that we must learn to bear what we cannot avoid. For Montaigne this was not resignation but rather an art of living in the body you have. Your irritation, fear and tiredness in illness are legitimate. And alongside them there can still be room for you yourself.
illness.practice: Today, notice a moment when the pain or weakness recedes even a little. Stay with it, as Montaigne did between attacks, and let yourself notice the relief.

pride.text: “To say less of yourself than is true is stupidity, not modesty,” Montaigne writes in “Of Practice,” following Aristotle. Your pride in what you’ve done is a good and honest feeling, and he wouldn’t shame you for it. He disliked both boasting and false modesty. Montaigne believed a person should know themselves accurately — neither exaggerating nor belittling. Healthy pride is simply accuracy: you did something, and that is true. At the same time Montaigne relied not on others’ praise but on his own testimony — on what he himself knew about his work and what it had cost. Let yourself be glad — calmly, without comparing yourself to others and without apologizing.
pride.practice: Describe what you did in one precise sentence — without “just,” “only” or “I got lucky.” Read it out loud.

quote.text: To say less of yourself than the truth is stupidity, not modesty.
quote.author: Michel de Montaigne

melancholy.text: The Essays began with melancholy: in “Of the Affection of Fathers for Their Children” Montaigne admits that the idea of taking up the pen came from solitude and a pensive, sad humour. Gentle melancholy, where sadness is mixed with tenderness, is weather he knew well. Yet Montaigne didn’t like heavy, oppressive sadness and didn’t consider it a virtue. But he knew well that our feelings are never pure: there is sadness in joy, and a sweetness of its own in sadness. Gentle melancholy is not a breakdown but a particular way of being attentive to life. A letter, a thought, a memory can be born of it. Montaigne turned it into a book. You can simply stay with it for a while.
melancholy.practice: Write one paragraph-“essay” about yourself today, starting from the mood rather than a topic — as Montaigne did.
